draft.title: A contested fossil record
card: Hominin fossils are rare and often broken. Scientists compare bone features to decide which species a fossil belongs to and how it is related to others.
A new find can change that picture. It may show that a feature appeared earlier or later than thought, or that a fossil sits in a different group.
Experts can disagree about the same bones. One may see a new species, while another sees a variation within a known one.
When evidence changes, the human family tree is refined or replaced. This is how science works: ideas are revised when better evidence appears.
draft.remember: A family tree is the best explanation for the evidence so far, and new fossils can change it.

a.q: Why can the hominin family tree change over time?
opts: New fossils can show features that do not fit the old tree
Scientists change the tree when they lose interest in it
Older fossils slowly change shape in the ground over time
Each new fossil must be placed on a new branch of the tree
a.why: The tree is built from evidence, so new evidence that does not fit can lead to changes. New fossils do not always need a new branch, and fossils do not change shape in the ground.
a.clue: Think about what a tree is built from.

b.q: Two experts study the same partial skull. One says it is a new species. The other says it is an unusual member of a known species. What does this show?
opts: The same fossil can be interpreted in different ways
One expert must have made an error in measuring
Fossils cannot be used as evidence of relationships
The skull should be left out of the family tree
b.why: Bones are often incomplete, so reasonable experts can read the same features differently. This does not mean anyone measured wrongly, and it does not make fossils useless. More evidence can later settle the question.
b.clue: Both experts could be using the evidence carefully.

a.best: New fossils can show features that do not fit the old tree

b.best: The same fossil can be interpreted in different ways

problems.detail: Why (a) says fossils do not change shape in the ground. This is false: fossils can be crushed or distorted during burial (taphonomic deformation). The distractor is wrong because this is not why the tree changes, not because fossils never deform.
The right option is the only hedged one ('can show'), while a distractor uses 'must'. A test-wise student could pick the hedged option without knowing the idea.
The right option is the only hedged one ('can be interpreted'), while the distractors use absolutes ('must', 'should', 'cannot'). This lets students pick it by wording alone.

a.q: What leads scientists to revise the hominin family tree?
opts: New finds give evidence that does not fit the current tree
Each new fossil is given its own new branch on the tree
A disagreement between two experts replaces the tree
Living humans keep evolving, so the old branches move
a.why: The tree is built from fossil evidence, so new finds that do not fit it lead to changes. A new fossil does not always need a new branch: it may fit a known species or move a fossil to a different group.
a.clue: Think about what the tree is built from.

b.q: Two experts study the same partial skull. One says it is a new species. The other says it is an unusual member of a known species. What does this show?
opts: Experts read the same bones in different ways

Fossils give no evidence about how species are related
The skull belongs outside the hominin family tree
b.why: Bones are often incomplete, so careful experts can read the same features differently. This does not mean anyone measured wrongly, and it does not make fossils useless as evidence. More finds can later help settle the question.
b.clue: Both experts could be using the evidence carefully.
